translations.text: The life and way of life of our holy father, honored in every way, Apa Onuphrius the hermit, who completed his life on the fourteenth day of the month of Paone, in the peace of God.
Bless us. Amen.
A brother who was a hermit, named Apa Paphnutius, related this to some God-loving brothers.
These are the words he spoke: “I, your brother, thought one day of going into the inner desert to see whether there was a brother monk farther on.
I walked for four days and four nights without eating bread or drinking water, traveling through the inner desert.
On the last day I came upon a cave.
When I approached it, I knocked at the door for about half a day, but no one answered me.
I thought to myself, ‘There is no brother here.’
But I saw a brother sitting there silently.
I took hold of his finger, but his finger crumbled in my hands and became like clods of earth.
I felt his whole body and found that he had been dead for a long time.
I looked and saw a tunic hanging up.
When I touched this too, it fell apart and turned to dust.
I stood up and prayed, and I took off my robe.
I wrapped it around him, dug in the earth with my hands, and buried him. Then I left that place.
I traveled farther into the desert and found another cave. I took courage and called into the doorway, but no one answered me.
I went inside and found no one. I came out, saying, ‘Wherever the servant of God is, he will come here.’
I stayed in that place, praying as the day went on.
I was also reciting the passages I had learned by heart.
Afterward, as the sun was about to set, I looked and saw a herd of antelopes coming from far away, with that brother among them.
As he approached me, he was naked, but his hair covered his private parts and served as clothing to cover him.
When he reached me, he became very frightened, thinking that I was a spirit. He stood still and prayed.
For many spirits had tempted him, as he told me afterward.
When I realized that he was afraid, I walked toward him.
I said to him, ‘Why are you afraid, servant of God?’
Look and see the soles of my feet, for I am human. Examine me, for I am flesh and blood.
When he looked into my face, he recited the prayer of the Gospel.
I urged him to take me down to his cave.
He asked me, “How did you come to this place?”
I said, “I came to this place wanting to see the servants of God who live in this desert, and God did not deprive me of what I was seeking.”
I asked him, “How did you come to this place? How long has it been since you came here? What did you used to eat? And why are you naked, with no clothing on you?”
He began speaking to me, saying, “I am a monk. I used to live in a community of monks in a monastery in the Thebaid.
A thought came into my heart like this: ‘Get up and leave. Settle in a place by yourself, and you will live in quiet and seclusion.
Welcome the brothers and be very hospitable to strangers, and you will gain a greater reward through the work of your hands.’
I did what I had thought of doing.
I left the monastery, built myself a dwelling apart, and settled in it.
A number of people commissioned handiwork from me, and I would give it as alms to strangers.
At that time the devil became jealous of the reward I was earning before the Lord for what I was doing for strangers
and others who were in need, seeing how diligently I applied myself to my handiwork.
He became very jealous of me because of what I was doing. He entered a nun who used to come to me and had commissioned some handiwork from me.
When I finished it, I gave it to her.
She spoke to me again about some more work. When we became accustomed to meeting each other, the enemy put it into my heart to accept handiwork from her.
When we became familiar with each other, we ate together.
Something became apparent to us, and in the end we struck the blow of death and brought forth lawlessness.
After I had foolishly fallen with her, we continued in this lawlessness for six months.
Afterward I reflected in my heart on what I had done. I became afraid, wept bitterly, and was in great anguish.
I reflected in my heart on what I had done. I became afraid, wept bitterly, and remained in great anguish.
I thought to myself in my heart, ‘Whether today or tomorrow, we will die, and we will be punished with harsh punishments:
the gnashing of teeth, the outer darkness, the unquenchable fire, and the sleepless worm that devours the soul.
Get up! Let us leave this place.’
Let us go into the desert.’
For my part, I chose to flee from sin.
I got up, left, and went into the wilderness.
And I gave up everything belonging to that woman.
I found this spring of water, this date palm, and this cave.
This date palm produces twelve clusters of dates each year, one cluster each month.
Each month, this cluster of dates is enough for me.
I have nothing else, neither clothing nor bread to eat.
My hair grew, and my clothes wore out completely.
So I covered with my hair the part that ought to be covered.
Now it has been thirty years since I came to this place. The air provides me with an even temperature, and I have eaten no bread at all.
I asked him, “When you first came to this place, did you suffer greatly?”
He said to me, “Yes, my son, I suffered greatly, so that I could not throw myself to the ground because of my anguish.”
“So that I could not throw myself to the ground because of my anguish, as I cried out to the Lord because of my many sins.
I also suffered great distress because of the [?] afflicting me.
I looked and saw a very glorious man. He stood beside me.
“He said to me, ‘What are you suffering from?’”
A little of my strength returned to me, and I said to him, ‘Sir, I am suffering in my liver.’
He said to me, ‘Show me the place where you are hurting.’
“I showed him where my liver was hurting.”
He stretched out his hand toward me, with his fingers held together, and cut open my side as though with a sword. He took out my liver and showed me the wounds on it.
He scraped them and put their pus on a cloth. Then he put my liver back in its place.
He stroked my body with his hands and joined together the place he had cut open.
He said to me, ‘Look, you are healed. Do not return to sin, so that something worse than this does not happen to you. Instead, serve the Lord from now on forever.’
From that day, all my internal organs were healed, and I stopped suffering from my liver.
I live in this desert place without suffering.”
He showed me the cloth with the pus on it.
I begged him to let me stay in the cave where I had first seen him.
He said to me, “You do not have the strength to withstand the assault of the demons.” And I begged him to tell me his name.
He said to me, “My name is Timothy.”
“Remember me, then, my beloved brother, so that the Lord may bring me to completion in the good struggle to which he has called me.”
I fell at his feet, asking him to remember me and bless me.
He blessed me, saying, “May the Lord bless you,
and save you from the devil’s snares, and keep you always in all his good paths, as you run toward the saints.”
When he had finished blessing me, my strength returned, so that I felt neither hunger nor thirst at all.
When I saw this great wonder that had happened to me, I got up and walked farther into the desert.
When four days had passed, I grew weary and stretched out my hands toward heaven.
I prayed, and there was the man who had come to me before.
He came to me again and strengthened me as he had the first time.
In short, the fourth day passed as I walked farther in.
Then I looked and saw a man in the distance, very frightening in appearance, with his hair spread over his body,
like a leopard’s, for he was naked, with leaves covering his private parts.
When he came near me, I became afraid.
I climbed onto a rocky hill, thinking that perhaps he was a wild donkey.
When he arrived, he lay down for a little while in the shade of a rocky hill. He was suffering terribly from the hardships he was enduring—hunger and thirst—and was in very grave danger.
He raised his eyes toward the rocky hill, saw me, and called out, “Come down here to me, holy man!
I too am a desert dweller like you, living in this wilderness because of my sins.”
He said to me, “You too are a friend of God.”
I sat down before him again and asked him to tell me his name.
He said to me, “My name is Onuphrius. I have now lived in this wilderness for sixty years, wandering through the mountains like the wild animals, and I have not seen anyone I knew.
I used to live in a community of monks in the desert near Hermopolis in the Thebaid.
The name of the monastery there is Erete.
We were all of one heart with one another, and peace prevailed among us. We lived together in quietness, giving glory to God.
I was a young [?] among them, learning from them to seek God. They were great men, perfected like the angels of the Lord.
I heard a story about our father Elijah the Tishbite, about how he became so strong through God while living in this desert.
And John the Baptist, than whom no one greater has arisen among those born of women, lived in the deserts until the day he appeared publicly in Israel.
I said to them, “My fathers, surely those in the desert are far better than we are?
For look: we see one another every day, and we gather together for worship.
If we are hungry, we have food prepared for us.
If we are thirsty, we have water to drink.
If we become weak, our brothers help us.
And if we desire a dish to eat, we serve it to one another out of love for God.
Where will those who live in the desert for God's sake find anyone if trouble overtakes them?
Or if they are hungry, where will they find food?
“‘If they are thirsty, where will they find water to drink?’
For at first, when they are about to withdraw into solitude, they rejoice greatly because of hunger and thirst and the disruptive activities
of the adversary, who fights against them to tempt them through these things, since he does not want them to remain in solitude.
He knows that the reward they will receive from God when they leave the body is great.
The very moment they persevere, God's mercies reach them. He has the angels serve them their food, and he brings them water out of a rock.
For it is written in Isaiah, ‘Those who wait patiently for the Lord will renew their strength.
They will grow wings like eagles.
They will run and not fall.
They will walk and not go hungry.’
He said, ‘They will bring them water out of a rock.’
And again, if they are hungry, he makes the plants in the fields taste sweet in their mouths, like sweet honey.
If trouble overtakes them or danger rises against them, they immediately stretch out their hands and pray to Jesus the King,
until his help reaches them swiftly, and he immediately drives them away and scatters them because their hearts are upright toward him.
Have you not heard what is written: ‘The Lord will not abandon his people,’ and, ‘The endurance of the poor will never perish’?
And again: “The poor man cried out.”
The Lord heard him.
He saved him from all his troubles.”
God gives each person according to the hardship he endures.
Blessed is the person who does God's will on earth.
I tell you, the angels will serve him while he is still in the body, and they will keep comforting him at all times in his troubles.
Now when I, the brother, heard these things from these perfected people of God, they became like sweet honey in my heart.
And a profound awareness arose within me.
I became like those whose minds have moved to the world to come.
I got up immediately.
I took a few loaves of bread with me, enough for four days of walking, to eat until I reached the place to which the Lord would direct me.
When I came out of my monastery, I looked.
I saw a light in front of me.
I was afraid.
I thought in my heart about turning back to the place where I had been before and remaining as I had been.
But when he realized that I was afraid, he said to me, "Do not be afraid.
I am the angel assigned to you, who has walked with you since your childhood.
This task that the Lord has assigned to you—you will [?] complete it."
When I entered the mountain, I walked through the desert for about six or seven miles.
I saw a cave.
I turned toward it to see whether anyone was in it.
A great holy man of God came out to me, beautiful in appearance, with great grace upon his face.
When I saw him, I bowed down before him.
But he raised me up.
He greeted me.
He said to me, "You are Onuphrius, my fellow worker in the Lord.
Come inside.
May the Lord be with you, and may you succeed in the good work to which he has called you."
I went inside.
I stayed with him for a few days.
I received instruction from him about godliness.
And he taught me how to carry out the work of the desert.
When he saw that I understood the hidden warfare and the terrors that exist in the desert, he said to me, “Get up, my son, let us go,
so that I may take you to a deserted place deep in the wilderness, where you can live alone for God’s sake,
since the Lord God has appointed you to this work, to live in the desert.”
Immediately he got up and walked with me into the desert, a journey of four days.
At the end of the four days, we came upon a small hut.
He said to me, “This is the place that the Lord has appointed for you to live in.”
He stayed with me for a month, until I understood the good work that I ought to do.
After that, he went away from me.
And we would see each other once a year, until the day he laid down his body.
And I buried him in the place where he was.
I said to him, “My dear, good father, how did you suffer when you first came to this place?”
The blessed old man said to me, “I suffered so much, time after time, from hunger and thirst, and from the blazing heat during the day and the great cold at night.
My flesh wasted away from the dew of heaven.
But when God [?] that I had persevered in the good struggle of fasting and that I had devoted myself to ascetic discipline,
he had the holy angels provide me with my daily food, giving it to me at night and sustaining my body.
And the date palm used to produce twelve bunches of dates for me each year, and I would eat one bunch each month.
He also made the other plants growing on the mountain taste sweet in my mouth, like honey.
For it is written, ‘A person will not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God—a person will live on these.’
If you do God’s will, he will take care of you everywhere.
For he said in the holy Gospel, ‘Do not worry about what you will eat or what you will drink,
or what you will wear. Your Father in heaven knows what you need before you ask him.
Instead, seek his kingdom and his righteousness.’”
And these things will be added to you.
When I heard these things, I was greatly amazed. I said to him, “O my holy father, where do you gather for worship on the Sabbath and on Sunday?”
He said to me, “O my holy father,
An angel of God comes to give me communion on the Sabbath and on Sunday. And everyone who lives in the desert for God’s sake and sees no one—
an angel comes to give them communion and comfort them.
And if they wish to see people, they are taken up to the heavens to see all the saints.
They greet them, and their hearts are filled with light. They rejoice and delight with God in the good things there.
When they see them, they are comforted and forget that they have suffered at all. Afterward they return to their bodies and remain comforted for a long time.
If they have been transported to the age to come through the joy they have seen, they no longer remember that a world exists.
When I heard this, I rejoiced greatly because I had been worthy to hear these things from him.
And I forgot all the hardships I had endured while traveling through the mountains.
Strength came into my body.
And a freshness came over my body and my soul.
I said to him, “Blessed am I, because I have been worthy to see your holy face and worthy to hear your sweet words.”
Then he said to me, “Get up, my brother, and let us go to the place where we stay.”
We got up.
We walked together for two or three miles. The way this blessed old man and champion walked was truly astonishing. We came upon a hut.
When we entered the hut, he stood up and prayed with me.
When we finished the prayer, we said, “Amen.”
Then we sat down together.
We continued talking about the greatness of God.
And when the sun was about to set, I looked
and saw a loaf of bread laid out, along with a vessel of water.
He said to me, “Get up, my brother, and eat, and drink some of this water, for I see that you are in danger from hunger, thirst, and the hardship of the journey.”
But I said to him, “As God Almighty lives, I will neither eat nor drink until we recline and eat together.”
When I kept urging him, we finally reclined together.
We broke the bread.
We ate.
We left some of it.
And both of us drank from the vessel of water.
We drank our fill and left some of it.
And we spent the whole night praying to God until dawn.
When morning came, I saw that his face had changed.
He was transformed, so that he looked like another person.
He looked entirely like fire.
And his appearance frightened me greatly.
He said to me, “Do not be afraid, my brother Paphnutius, for the Lord has sent you to take care of my body and bury it.
For today I will complete my service and go to the place of eternal rest.”
That day was the sixteenth of the month of Paone.
He also said to me, “When you go to Egypt, proclaim my remembrance as a sweet fragrance for the brothers.
Whoever gives an offering in my name in remembrance of me, Jesus himself will bring him in at the first hour of the thousand years.”
I said to him, “What if he is poor and cannot give an offering in your name?”
He said to me, “Let him feed a poor brother in my name.”
He said to me, “If he is poor and cannot feed him, will you not bring him to the banquet at the first hour of the thousand years?”
He said to me, “Let him offer a little incense in my name.”
I said to him, “What if he is poor and cannot offer incense in your name because of his poverty?
Yes, my good father, may your mercy reach us all, for whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”
He said to me, “Let him stand and pray to God three times in my name, and the Lord Jesus will bring him into the thousand years, and he will inherit with all the saints.”
I said to him, “O my holy father, if I am worthy, I want to remain in your holy place when you leave this body.”
He said to me, “No, my son.
For you have not been appointed to this service. Rather, the Lord has appointed you to comfort the holy brothers who live in the desert,
so that you may proclaim them and their sweet fragrance among the brothers who serve God, for the benefit of those who hear.
Go away to Egypt, my son, and persevere in good work.”
Immediately I fell to the ground.
I said to him, “Bless me, my father, so that mercy may reach me in God's presence.
Just as I have been worthy to see you on earth, may I also be worthy to see you in the age to come, beside the Lord Jesus Christ.”
He said to me, “My son, God will not grieve you in anything. He will strengthen you in his love,
and your eyes will receive light through his divinity. You will neither turn aside nor fall, but you will succeed in the work you have undertaken.”
May the angels protect you and rescue you from the plots of the Jews, so that they find no grounds for accusing you when you meet God.
When he had finished saying these things, he stood up.
He prayed to God with sighs and many tears.
Afterward, he lay down on the ground.
He completed the task God had given him and entrusted his spirit into God's hands on the sixteenth day of the month of Paone.
I heard the voices of angels singing hymns before the blessed Apa Onuphrius, and there was great joy as he went to meet God.
I stripped myself of the cloak I was wearing.
I gave half of it for the burial, and I covered myself with the other half so that I would not remain naked.
I laid his body down in the cleft of a rock.
I heard the sound of a multitude of angels rejoicing and crying out, “Hallelujah!”
I offered my prayer over him and piled many stones over him.
I stood up.
I prayed a second time, and immediately the palm tree fell.
I was utterly amazed at what had happened.
I ate what was left of the bread and drank the water that had been left for us.
When I saw that it was not God's will for me to remain in that place, I stretched out my hands.
I prayed to the Lord, and look, the man who had first come to me and strengthened me came to me again as before.
He said to me, “Paphnutius, our Lord told us today that you were coming to us here.
For a hundred years we have seen no human being except you alone.”
After we had spent a long time talking with one another,
we finally said to him, “Our brother, refresh yourself with a little bread, because you have come a long way.
The Lord has appointed us to stay together for a day.
We rejoice with you, our beloved brother.”
While we were talking with one another, look, five loaves were brought in, warm and fresh, as though they had just been taken out of the oven.
Immediately, something else to eat was also brought.
We sat down and ate together.
And he said to me, “This is the sixth year since we came to this place.
Four loaves are allotted to us each day, brought to us by God.
But today, when you came to us, look, a fifth was brought for you.
We never know where they have come from; we simply come in and find them laid out.”
When we had finished eating together, we spent the whole night praying until dawn.
When morning came, I begged them to let me stay with them until the day of my death.
They said to me, “Our brother, it has not been appointed for you to remain here.
Instead, get up and go to Egypt, and tell the brothers what you have seen, as a reminder to them and for the benefit of those who hear.
I begged them to tell me their names, but they would not agree to tell them.
I pressed them, but still they did not tell me their names.
They answered, “The one who gave a name to everything and knows all things is the one who knows our names.
Now then, our brother, remember us until we see you in the house of God.
Be diligent, and do not let the world deceive you, for it has deceived many.”
When they had finished saying these things, they blessed me and embraced me.
I left them.
When I was a day’s walk away from them, I came upon a spring of water.
I sat down for a little while because I was tired. There were large trees growing beside the spring.
After I had lain down and rested a little, I kept gazing at the trees in amazement,
wondering who had planted them in this place.
Among them were date palms laden with fruit, citron trees, pomegranate trees, and fig trees,
as well as apple trees, grapevines, peach trees, [?], and other trees giving off a sweet fragrance.
The spring poured out streams of water, watering all the trees growing in that place.
While I was marveling at the trees and looking at them and their fruit,
four young boys came from a distance, beautiful in appearance, wearing beautiful palm leaves wrapped around them like loincloths.
When they reached me, they said to me, “Greetings, Paphnutius, our beloved brother!”
But I bowed down
and paid homage to them.
But they raised me up
and greeted me.
They were filled with great amazement, like people who had passed into the next age, in their joy and the comfort they gave me.
They kept picking fruit from the trees and putting it into my mouth.
My heart rejoiced because of the loving care they showed me.
For I spent seven days with them, eating the fruit of the trees.
I asked them, “Where did you come from to this place? And where are you from?”
They said to him, “Our brother, God has sent you to us. We will tell you our whole life story.
For we are from a city in Egypt called Oxyrhynchus.
Our fathers were city councilors, and we were sent to school to be educated.
We were together in the same school, and we were of one heart.
After we had been educated at school, we were sent to the [?], after they had educated us
well in every discipline and all the wisdom of this world. But now we wanted to be educated in the wisdom of God.
One day, as we were speaking with one another about these things, a good thought began to work in our inner being.
The four of us got up
and went into the mountain to live in solitude until we could see what the Lord would appoint for us.
We took a few loaves of bread with us, enough for seven days.
When we had gone far into the mountain, a trance immediately came over us.
A man who was entirely radiant took us by the hand
and brought us to this place.
When we came to this place, we found a holy man of God, and the angel of the Lord entrusted us to him.
He continued teaching us to serve God for a whole year.
At the end of the year, the holy, blessed old man passed away.
We are the only ones living here, our master and brother.
Look, we declare to you before the Lord that for sixty years we have not known the taste of bread or any other food except these trees alone, living on their fruit.
For when we want to see one another, we come here each week to see one another.
We spend the whole night before Sunday together. Afterward, each of us goes away to follow his way of life.
I said to them, “Where do you receive communion?”
They said to me, “We gather here for this purpose, because every Saturday an angel of God comes and gives us communion on Saturday and Sunday.”
I stayed with them, rejoicing greatly.
“On the seventh day an angel of the Lord will come and give us communion together with you.
Anyone who receives communion through that angel will be cleansed of every sin, and no adversary will be able to overpower him.”
While we were talking with one another, I smelled a powerful fragrance, the like of which I had never smelled before.
As soon as the fragrance reached us, we rose, stood up, and praised God.
Afterward, an angel came.
He gave us communion together in the body and blood of the Lord.
I became like someone in a stupor because of the terrifying sight I had seen.
He blessed us.
He went up to heaven while we followed him with our eyes.
After he had gone, they brought me back to my senses.
They said to me, “Be firm, take courage, and be a strong man.”
Immediately I came to my senses, like someone sobering up from wine.
We spent the whole night before Sunday standing in prayer until dawn.
When daylight appeared early on Sunday, there again was the sweet fragrance, and we smelled it.
We took pleasure in it and rejoiced like those in the world to come.
Afterward, the angel came.
He gave us communion and blessed each of us, saying, “May it be eternal life for you, and an imperishable prophecy.”
All of us together answered with one voice, “Amen. May it be so.”
Afterward, the angel turned toward me.
He said to me, “Get up and set out for Egypt, and tell the brothers who love God what you have seen, so that they may strive to imitate the way of life of the saints.”
I begged him to let me stay with them.
He said to me, “The Lord has not assigned us all the same work to do. Rather, God gives to each person according to what he can bear.”
“Now, then, get up and go, for this is the way he has appointed for you.”
And he blessed me.
He went to heaven in glory.
Then they brought a great deal of fruit.
We ate together.
Then I left them, and they accompanied me for six miles.
I asked them, “Tell me your names.”
They each told me their names.
The first was John.
The second was Andrew.
The third was Heraclammon.
The fourth was Theophilus.
They instructed me to tell their names to the brothers so that they would remember them.
I, in turn, begged them to remember me.
Then we prayed and greeted one another.
I went away deeply saddened.
But I was rejoicing because of the blessing the saints had given me.
I reached Egypt after a three-day journey on foot.
When I found the brothers who love God, I rested with them for ten days.
I told them what had happened to me.
They said, “Truly, you have been found worthy of a great gift.”
For the brothers there loved God. They were spiritual warriors who served God with all their heart, and their dwelling place was Scetis.
They quickly wrote down these words that they had heard from Apa Paphnutius.
They quickly put them into a book.
They sent it to Scetis.
They placed the account in the church for the benefit of those who would hear it.
They spoke about it, and it served as a meditation for them, on everyone’s lips.
They glorified God and blessed his saints through the grace and love for humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Through whom, glory be to him and his good Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever.
Amen.
I, Victor, the least of deacons, son of the blessed Mercurius, deacon of Saint Mercurius the great general, from the city of Latopolis, wrote this book.
Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.
It was written on the third day of the month of Tobe, in the year 721 of the holy martyrs, in the third indiction.
Through the diligence and care of our fathers and beloved brothers, Abba Abraham, the superior appointed by God, and the archdeacon Abba Chael,
and the deputy superior Zechariah, the deacon and monk of the monastery of Saint Mercurius the general, which is on the mountain of Tbo.
They produced this book through their own labor.
They placed it in their monastery so that it might be read for the benefit and full assurance of those who read it and anyone who listens to it attentively, so that our good Savior
and Saint Apa Onuphrius the hermit may bless them and the entire community of their monastery with the blessing of heaven and the blessing of the earth in all their fullness.
May he establish lasting blessing, abundance, peace, and salvation in their monastery.
May he save them from the snares of the devil and from evil people.
And when they leave the body, according to what is appointed for every person,
may they hear: “Well done, good and faithful servants! Since you have been faithful over a few things, I will put you in charge of many. Enter into the joy of your master.”
And may they be worthy to receive an inheritance with all the saints. Amen. So be it.
